clinicalPearls: Inherited qualitative fibrinogen defect in which a structurally abnormal molecule is produced, so fibrinogen is present in normal or near-normal amount but functions poorly.
Caused by variants in one of the three fibrinogen genes, FGA, FGB or FGG, and usually inherited in an autosomal dominant manner.
Clinically heterogeneous: many patients are asymptomatic, some bleed, and a substantial subset paradoxically have a thrombotic tendency.
The diagnostic hallmark is a low functional (Clauss) fibrinogen with a discordantly normal or near-normal antigenic fibrinogen level, giving a reduced activity-to-antigen ratio.
Thrombin time and reptilase time are typically prolonged, reflecting defective fibrinopeptide release or abnormal fibrin polymerisation.
Certain specific variants are strongly associated with venous or arterial thrombosis rather than bleeding, so family and variant context guides risk.
Distinguish from hypodysfibrinogenaemia (low activity and low antigen) and from acquired dysfibrinogenaemia of liver disease.
Management is individualised and event-driven rather than routinely prophylactic, balancing the patient's bleeding versus thrombotic phenotype, with particular vigilance in pregnancy and surgery.
reference.pathophysiology: Congenital dysfibrinogenaemia is a disorder of fibrinogen quality rather than quantity. Fibrinogen is a hexameric plasma glycoprotein assembled from paired Aalpha, Bbeta and gamma chains encoded by FGA, FGB and FGG; upon activation, thrombin cleaves fibrinopeptides A and B to expose polymerisation sites, allowing fibrin monomers to assemble into a branching network that is then covalently stabilised by factor XIIIa. Pathogenic missense variants, most often clustered in functionally critical regions such as the thrombin cleavage sites of the Aalpha chain or the polymerisation and cross-linking domains of the gamma chain, produce a circulating molecule that is antigenically present but functionally impaired. Depending on the site of the defect, the abnormal fibrinogen may show delayed or defective fibrinopeptide release, impaired fibrin monomer polymerisation, abnormal cross-linking, defective calcium or thrombin binding, or altered susceptibility to fibrinolysis. This mechanistic diversity explains the strikingly variable phenotype: variants that chiefly slow clot formation tend toward a bleeding tendency, whereas those that yield an abnormally rigid clot resistant to plasmin-mediated lysis, or that impair the normal antithrombin function of fibrin, predispose to thrombosis. Because the antigen level is preserved, standard clot-based fibrinogen assays underestimate the true protein mass, producing the characteristic dissociation between low functional activity and normal immunological concentration that defines the disorder.
additionalDifferentials: Congenital afibrinogenaemia and hypofibrinogenaemia (quantitative fibrinogen deficiencies)
Congenital hypodysfibrinogenaemia with both reduced function and reduced antigen
Acquired dysfibrinogenaemia of chronic liver disease or hepatocellular carcinoma
Other inherited thrombophilias when the presentation is thrombotic
Other inherited bleeding disorders such as factor XIII deficiency when the presentation is bleeding
Disseminated intravascular coagulation with consumptive fibrinogen abnormalities
Direct thrombin inhibitor or heparin effect prolonging thrombin time
additionalInvestigations: Clauss functional fibrinogen assay alongside immunological (antigen) fibrinogen to demonstrate a reduced activity-to-antigen ratio
Thrombin time and reptilase time, characteristically prolonged
Prothrombin time and activated partial thromboplastin time for context
Molecular genetic analysis of FGA, FGB and FGG to identify the causative variant and inform phenotype
Family studies and cascade testing given autosomal dominant inheritance
Fibrinogen function studies such as fibrin polymerisation or clot structure analysis in specialist laboratories
Liver function tests to exclude an acquired cause
redFlags: Unexplained venous or arterial thrombosis, especially in a young patient or with a suggestive family history
Significant or unexpected bleeding during surgery, trauma or the peripartum period
Postpartum haemorrhage or recurrent pregnancy loss and placental complications
Poor wound healing or delayed clotting after invasive procedures
Combined bleeding and thrombotic events in the same individual indicating a high-risk variant
reference.prognosis: Many individuals remain asymptomatic with a normal lifespan, and outcomes depend heavily on the specific variant and whether the phenotype is bleeding, thrombotic or mixed. With informed, event-directed management around surgery, pregnancy and acute events, most patients do well, though high-risk variants carry appreciable morbidity from recurrent thrombosis or serious haemorrhage.
pitfalls: Overlooking the diagnosis when total (antigenic) fibrinogen is reported as normal; the functional assay must be examined.
Assuming all patients bleed and giving inappropriate prophylaxis to those with a thrombotic variant, or vice versa.
Confusing congenital disease with acquired dysfibrinogenaemia of liver disease without checking hepatic function and history.
Relying on prothrombin-time-derived fibrinogen, which may not reveal the qualitative defect.
Failing to plan individualised peri-operative and pregnancy management with a specialist haemostasis service.
references: Standard clinical haematology and haemostasis textbooks
International Society on Thrombosis and Haemostasis guidance on rare coagulation disorders
National haemophilia and rare bleeding disorder guidelines
management: Tailor management to the individual phenotype (asymptomatic, bleeding or thrombotic), guided by the specific FGA/FGB/FGG variant and family history rather than the fibrinogen level alone
For bleeding phenotypes, use fibrinogen replacement with fibrinogen concentrate or cryoprecipitate around surgery, trauma and delivery to secure haemostasis
For thrombosis-associated variants, treat venous or arterial events with anticoagulation and consider long-term anticoagulation according to recurrence risk
Use antifibrinolytic agents such as tranexamic acid for mucosal bleeding or as a surgical adjunct where appropriate
Plan pregnancy and peripartum care jointly with haematology, since both bleeding and thrombotic complications including placental problems can occur, and consider thromboprophylaxis
Provide peri-operative haemostatic planning and issue a patient alert card documenting the disorder
Offer genetic counselling and cascade testing given autosomal dominant inheritance, and refer to a specialist coagulation centre
